extracted.intended_audience: reporters, editors and producers working on tight deadlines (journalists covering trauma)
extracted.subtask_description: A concise style guide for journalists on ethical, evidence-informed reporting about trauma, including language usage, news choices, and special considerations for trauma-laden topics (e.g., sexual violence, racism). Designed for rapid reference on deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concise, authoritative guidance for on-deadline reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: This style guide is designed as a quick, authoritative reference for reporters, editors and producers working on tight deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries are concise and intended for rapid use in breaking news, features, photographs and other fast-paced newsroom contexts. Prioritize clear, actionable recommendations over long theoretical exposition when helping journalists on deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-informed guidance on news choices, language and ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes brief evidence-informed guidance on news choices, language usage and ethics in reporting on the impact of trauma on individuals, families and communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations should be grounded in trauma science and/or accumulated journalistic expertise; where evidence exists, cite or base guidance on consensus findings. Cover practical newsroom choices as well as ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of psychological and scientific terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides recommendations for appropriate use of relevant psychological and scientific terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid casual or imprecise diagnostic language; use clinical terms only when accurate and supported by evidence or authoritative sources. Explain terms when necessary for reader understanding and avoid sensationalizing scientific concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special considerations for trauma-laden topics (e.g., racism, sexual violence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes special considerations when reporting on consequential trauma-laden issues such as racism and sexual violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the distinctive harms, sensitivities and ethical complexities of different trauma contexts. Adapt interviewing, sourcing, framing and language to the specific nature of the trauma-laden issue being covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline recommendations grounded in evidence and practitioner expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: All entries reflect the Dart Center’s baseline recommendations for best practice; entries rooted in trauma science are grounded in evidence-based consensus among experts, while reporting-practice entries reflect accumulated recommendations of experienced journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish where guidance is evidence-based versus drawn from journalistic practice. Where possible, link to supporting research, expert consensus, or exemplar journalistic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor guidelines and recommendations over rigid commandments
rubrics_metrics.description: While some guidance is stringent (e.g. limited circumstances to refer to PTSD), the guide emphasizes guidelines and recommendations over rigid commandments, recognizing fluid and assignment-specific decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage trauma-informed critical thinking rather than inflexible adherence to rules; provide context and caveats so journalists can adapt guidance to particular assignments and cultural contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict and clarify use of diagnostic labels (e.g., PTSD)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some areas the guidance is stringent — for instance, the limited circumstances in which it is accurate to refer to Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagnostic labels only when medically diagnosed or when reporting on clinical assessment; avoid casual application of psychiatric diagnoses to behaviors or reactions that may be normal responses to trauma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the guide as a living, updateable resource with links to deeper material
rubrics_metrics.description: The Dart Center Style Guide is a living document, designed to be regularly expanded and updated to reflect evolving best practices and scientific understanding; entries link to the Dart Center’s online library and other authoritative resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep entries current, add new topics as evidence and practice evolve, and include links to in-depth tip sheets, backgrounders and peer resources for journalists who need deeper guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge cultural, linguistic and positional bias and pursue intersectionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Any journalism stylebook reflects time, place and culture; the guide attempts to reflect global, cross-cultural and intersectional perspectives but acknowledges its Anglophone, U.S.-based authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about cultural and linguistic limitations of guidance, adapt recommendations to local contexts, incorporate intersectional perspectives, and solicit feedback from diverse communities and practitioners to improve relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize guidance by thematic sections and alphabetically for rapid lookup
rubrics_metrics.description: The guide is organized in four thematic sections (Trauma Science and Psychology; Violence and Aftermath; Identity; Community and Social Issues) with entries alphabetical within sections and links to related resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure a style guide so journalists can quickly find terms and topics; include cross-links between related entries and provide navigational tips (e.g., use browser FIND) for rapid reference during reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists should have baseline literacy in trauma concepts and reporting standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsible reporting and newsroom decision-making now demand baseline literacy in trauma concepts and emerging reporting standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should cultivate basic understanding of how violence, abuse, conflict and chronic threat affect individuals and communities; this literacy should inform interviewing, sourcing, story selection, framing and editorial decisions.
